title: The Precise Definition of a Limit
short: The Precise Definition of a Limit
lead: The intuitive idea of a limit is made precise: a distance ε from the limit and a distance δ from the point approached say exactly how close is close. The definition is put to work proving statements about limits, proving a limit law, showing that a limit does not exist, and defining one-sided and infinite limits.
objectives: Describe the epsilon-delta definition of a limit.
Apply the epsilon-delta definition to find the limit of a function.
Describe the epsilon-delta definitions of one-sided limits and infinite limits.
Use the epsilon-delta definition to prove the limit laws.
summary_html:
• The intuitive notion of a limit may be converted into a rigorous mathematical definition known as the epsilon-delta definition of the limit.
  • The epsilon-delta definition may be used to prove statements about limits.
  • The epsilon-delta definition of a limit may be modified to define one-sided limits.

exercises.prompt:
The following graph of the function f satisfies $\lim_{x\to 3}f(x)=2.$ In the following exercises, for each value of $\varepsilon$, find a value of $\delta\gt 0$ such that the precise definition of limit holds true.

$\varepsilon=3$

[T] In the following exercises, use a graphing calculator to find a number $\delta$ such that the statements hold true.

$|\sqrt{x-4}-2|\lt 0.1,\;\text{whenever}\;|x-8|\lt\delta$

In the following exercises, use the precise definition of limit to prove the given limits.

$\lim_{x\to 2}(5x+8)=18$

In the following exercises, use the precise definition of limit to prove the given limits.

$\lim_{x\to 3}\frac{x^{2}-9}{x-3}=6$

In the following exercises, use the precise definition of limit to prove the given limits.

$\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{2x^{2}-3x-2}{x-2}=5$

answer.solution: For $x\ne 2,$ $\frac{2x^{2}-3x-2}{x-2}=\frac{(2x+1)(x-2)}{x-2}=2x+1.$ Let $\varepsilon\gt 0.$ Choose $\delta=\varepsilon/2.$ Assume $0\lt|x-2|\lt\delta;$ then $x\ne 2,$ so $\left|\frac{2x^{2}-3x-2}{x-2}-5\right|=|2x+1-5|=2|x-2|\lt 2\delta=\varepsilon.$ Therefore, $\lim_{x\to 2}\frac{2x^{2}-3x-2}{x-2}=5.$

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, use the precise definition of limit to prove the given limits.

$\lim_{x\to 0}x^{4}=0$

In the following exercises, use the precise definition of limit to prove the given limits.

$\lim_{x\to 2}(x^{2}+2x)=8$

answer.solution: Let $\varepsilon\gt 0.$ Choose $\delta=\min\{1,\varepsilon/7\}.$ Assume $0\lt|x-2|\lt\delta.$ Since $|x-2|\lt 1,$ we have $1\lt x\lt 3,$ so $5\lt x+4\lt 7$ and $|x+4|\lt 7.$ Then $|(x^{2}+2x)-8|=|x-2|\cdot|x+4|\lt\frac{\varepsilon}{7}\cdot 7=\varepsilon.$ Therefore, $\lim_{x\to 2}(x^{2}+2x)=8.$

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, use the precise definition of limit to prove the given one-sided limits.

$\lim_{x\to 5^{-}}\sqrt{5-x}=0$

In the following exercises, use the precise definition of limit to prove the given one-sided limits.

$\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}f(x)=-2,\;\text{where}\;f(x)=\begin{cases}8x-3, & \text{if}\;x\lt 0\\ 4x-2, & \text{if}\;x\ge 0\end{cases}.$

answer.solution: Let $\varepsilon\gt 0.$ Choose $\delta=\varepsilon/4.$ Assume $0\lt x-0\lt\delta.$ Since $x\gt 0,$ $f(x)=4x-2,$ so $|f(x)-(-2)|=|4x|=4x\lt 4\delta=\varepsilon.$ Therefore, $\lim_{x\to 0^{+}}f(x)=-2.$ Only the values of $f$ to the right of 0 enter, so the piece $8x-3$ plays no part.

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, use the precise definition of limit to prove the given one-sided limits.

$\lim_{x\to 1^{-}}f(x)=3,\;\text{where}\;f(x)=\begin{cases}5x-2, & \text{if}\;x\lt 1\\ 7x-1, & \text{if}\;x\ge 1\end{cases}.$

In the following exercises, use the precise definition of limit to prove the given infinite limits.

$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{x^{2}}=\infty$

answer.solution: Let $M\gt 0.$ Choose $\delta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}.$ Assume $0\lt|x-0|\lt\delta.$ Then $0\lt x^{2}\lt\delta^{2}=\frac{1}{M},$ so $\frac{1}{x^{2}}\gt M.$ Therefore, $\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1}{x^{2}}=\infty.$

exercises.prompt:
In the following exercises, use the precise definition of limit to prove the given infinite limits.

$\lim_{x\to -1}\frac{3}{(x+1)^{2}}=\infty$

In the following exercises, use the precise definition of limit to prove the given infinite limits.

$\lim_{x\to 2}-\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}=-\infty$

answer.solution: Let $M\gt 0.$ Choose $\delta=\frac{1}{\sqrt{M}}.$ Assume $0\lt|x-2|\lt\delta.$ Then $0\lt(x-2)^{2}\lt\frac{1}{M},$ so $\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}\gt M$ and $-\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}\lt -M.$ Therefore, $\lim_{x\to 2}-\frac{1}{(x-2)^{2}}=-\infty.$

If there is a maximum error tolerance in the area of 8 cm2, how accurately must the engineer cut on the side, assuming all sides have the same length? How do these numbers relate to $\delta,$ $\varepsilon$, a, and L?

answer.solution: The engineer must cut within 0.328 cm of 12 cm on each side; $\varepsilon=8,\delta=0.328,a=12,L=144$

exercises.prompt: Use the precise definition of limit to prove that the following limit does not exist: $\lim_{x\to 1}\frac{|x-1|}{x-1}.$

answer.solution: The function is $-1$ for $x\lt 1$ and $1$ for $x\gt 1.$ Suppose $L$ is a candidate for the limit. Choose $\varepsilon=1/2,$ and let $\delta\gt 0.$ If $L\ge 0,$ let $x=1-\delta/2:$ then $0\lt|x-1|=\delta/2\lt\delta$ and $\left|\frac{|x-1|}{x-1}-L\right|=|-1-L|=L+1\ge 1\gt\frac{1}{2}=\varepsilon.$ If $L\lt 0,$ let $x=1+\delta/2:$ then $0\lt|x-1|\lt\delta$ and $|1-L|=|L|+1\ge 1\gt\varepsilon.$ So for every $L$ there is an $\varepsilon$ that no $\delta$ meets, and $\lim_{x\to 1}\frac{|x-1|}{x-1}$ does not exist.

exercises.prompt: Using precise definitions of limits, prove that $\lim_{x\to 0}f(x)$ does not exist, given that $f(x)$ is the ceiling function. (Hint: Try any $\delta\lt 1.$)

answer.solution: The ceiling function is $0$ for $-1\lt x\le 0$ and $1$ for $0\lt x\le 1.$ Suppose $L$ is a candidate for the limit. Choose $\varepsilon=1/2,$ let $\delta\gt 0,$ and set $d=\min\{\delta,1\}.$ If $L\ge 1/2,$ let $x=-d/2:$ then $0\lt|x|\lt\delta$ and $|f(x)-L|=|0-L|=L\ge\frac{1}{2}=\varepsilon.$ If $L\lt 1/2,$ let $x=d/2:$ then $0\lt|x|\lt\delta$ and $|f(x)-L|=1-L\gt\frac{1}{2}=\varepsilon.$ Either way some $x$ within $\delta$ of 0 has $|f(x)-L|\ge\varepsilon,$ so no $L$ is the limit and $\lim_{x\to 0}f(x)$ does not exist.

exercises.prompt: Using precise definitions of limits, prove that $\lim_{x\to 0}f(x)$ does not exist: $f(x)=\begin{cases}1 & \text{if}\;x\;\text{is rational}\\ 0 & \text{if}\;x\;\text{is irrational}\end{cases}.$ (Hint: Think about how you can always choose a rational number $0\lt r\lt d,$ but $|f(r)-0|=1.$)

answer.solution: Suppose $L$ is a candidate for the limit. Choose $\varepsilon=1/2,$ and let $\delta\gt 0.$ Between 0 and $\delta$ there are both a rational number $r$ and an irrational number $s,$ so $0\lt|r|\lt\delta,$ $0\lt|s|\lt\delta,$ $f(r)=1$ and $f(s)=0.$ If $L\ge 1/2,$ then $|f(s)-L|=L\ge\varepsilon;$ if $L\lt 1/2,$ then $|f(r)-L|=1-L\gt\varepsilon.$ Either way some $x$ within $\delta$ of 0 has $|f(x)-L|\ge\varepsilon,$ so $\lim_{x\to 0}f(x)$ does not exist.

exercises.prompt: Using precise definitions of limits, determine $\lim_{x\to 0}f(x)$ for $f(x)=\begin{cases}x & \text{if}\;x\;\text{is rational}\\ 0 & \text{if}\;x\;\text{is irrational}\end{cases}.$ (Hint: Break into two cases, x rational and x irrational.)
Using the function from the previous exercise, use the precise definition of limits to show that $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ does not exist for $a\ne 0.$

answer.solution: Here $f(x)=x$ for rational $x$ and $f(x)=0$ for irrational $x,$ and $a\ne 0.$ Suppose $L$ is a candidate for the limit. Choose $\varepsilon=|a|/4,$ and let $\delta\gt 0.$ If $|L|\ge|a|/4,$ pick an irrational $x$ with $0\lt|x-a|\lt\delta:$ then $|f(x)-L|=|L|\ge\varepsilon.$ If $|L|\lt|a|/4,$ pick a rational $x$ with $0\lt|x-a|\lt\min\{\delta,|a|/2\}:$ then $|x|\gt|a|/2,$ so $|f(x)-L|=|x-L|\ge|x|-|L|\gt\frac{|a|}{2}-\frac{|a|}{4}=\varepsilon.$ Either way some $x$ within $\delta$ of $a$ has $|f(x)-L|\ge\varepsilon,$ so $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)$ does not exist.

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, suppose that $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ and $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=M$ both exist. Use the precise definition of limits to prove the following limit laws:

$\lim_{x\to a}(f(x)+g(x))=L+M$

For the following exercises, suppose that $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ and $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=M$ both exist. Use the precise definition of limits to prove the following limit laws:

$\lim_{x\to a}[cf(x)]=cL$ for any real constant c (Hint: Consider two cases: $c=0$ and $c\ne 0.$)

answer.solution: If $c=0,$ then $cf(x)=0=cL$ for every $x,$ so $|cf(x)-cL|=0\lt\varepsilon$ for any $\varepsilon\gt 0$ and any $\delta.$ If $c\ne 0,$ let $\varepsilon\gt 0.$ Since $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L,$ choose $\delta\gt 0$ so that if $0\lt|x-a|\lt\delta,$ then $|f(x)-L|\lt\frac{\varepsilon}{|c|}.$ Assume $0\lt|x-a|\lt\delta.$ Then $|cf(x)-cL|=|c|\,|f(x)-L|\lt|c|\cdot\frac{\varepsilon}{|c|}=\varepsilon.$ Therefore, $\lim_{x\to a}[cf(x)]=cL.$

exercises.prompt:
For the following exercises, suppose that $\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=L$ and $\lim_{x\to a}g(x)=M$ both exist. Use the precise definition of limits to prove the following limit laws:

$\lim_{x\to a}[f(x)g(x)]=LM.$ (Hint: $|f(x)g(x)-LM|=|f(x)g(x)-f(x)M+f(x)M-LM|\le|f(x)||g(x)-M|+|M||f(x)-L|.$)

answer.solution: Let $\varepsilon\gt 0.$ Choose $\delta_{1}\gt 0$ so that $0\lt|x-a|\lt\delta_{1}$ gives $|f(x)-L|\lt 1,$ and so $|f(x)|\lt|L|+1.$ Choose $\delta_{2}\gt 0$ so that $0\lt|x-a|\lt\delta_{2}$ gives $|g(x)-M|\lt\frac{\varepsilon}{2(|L|+1)},$ and $\delta_{3}\gt 0$ so that $0\lt|x-a|\lt\delta_{3}$ gives $|f(x)-L|\lt\frac{\varepsilon}{2(|M|+1)}.$ Choose $\delta=\min\{\delta_{1},\delta_{2},\delta_{3}\}$ and assume $0\lt|x-a|\lt\delta.$ By the hint, $|f(x)g(x)-LM|\le|f(x)||g(x)-M|+|M||f(x)-L|\lt(|L|+1)\cdot\frac{\varepsilon}{2(|L|+1)}+|M|\cdot\frac{\varepsilon}{2(|M|+1)}\lt\frac{\varepsilon}{2}+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}=\varepsilon.$ Therefore, $\lim_{x\to a}[f(x)g(x)]=LM.$

assumes.text: Since $\lim_{x\to a}\kf(x)=\kL$, there is a $\delta_{1}\gt 0$ so that if $0\lt|x-a|\lt\delta_{1}$, then $|\kf(x)-\kL|\lt\varepsilon/2$.
Since $\lim_{x\to a}\kg(x)=M$, there is a $\delta_{2}\gt 0$ so that if $0\lt|x-a|\lt\delta_{2}$, then $|\kg(x)-M|\lt\varepsilon/2$.
$\lim_{x\to a}\kf(x)=\kL$ if, for every $\varepsilon\gt 0$, there exists a $\delta\gt 0$ such that if $0\lt|x-a|\lt\delta$, then $|\kf(x)-\kL|\lt\varepsilon$.

steps.cap: The $\varepsilon\gt 0$ was any, and $\delta=\min\{\delta_{1},\delta_{2}\}$ answers it, which is what the definition asks.
